claims.text: Introducing a Ti-rich Heusler-type or ordered B2 secondary phase into an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti high-entropy alloy will locally enhance the orbital magnetic moment at the phase interface.
The interfacial orbital-moment enhancement will increase coercivity above 100 Oe.
A secondary Heusler-type or B2 phase can be introduced while retaining an fcc matrix.
The secondary phase will create a magnetic pinning landscape distinct from the behavior of the bulk single-phase alloy.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti has suppressed orbital moments and coercivity below 100 Oe.
The suppressed orbital moment and low coercivity arise from a delocalized magnetic ground state in the fcc structure.
Annealing at 900°C for 50 hours can generate a Ti-containing Heusler-type or B2 secondary phase.
The proposed heat treatment will produce coherent or semi-coherent interfaces between the fcc matrix and the secondary phase.
The fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix will remain stable from 300 K to 600 K.
The Ti-rich secondary phase will retain an ordered magnetic structure from 300 K to 600 K.
The fcc/secondary-phase interface will act as a magnetic domain-wall pinning site.
Chemical ordering in the secondary phase will break local fcc symmetry and enhance the interfacial orbital moment.
The secondary phase has a distinct magnetic ground state with greater orbital-moment anisotropy than the fcc matrix.
Interaction between the fcc matrix and the secondary phase creates an interfacial strain field and chemical-potential gradient.
The interfacial strain field and chemical-potential gradient suppress the magnetic-entropy contribution to stacking-fault energy, analogously to local-spin-fluctuation effects in CoCrFeMnNi.
Suppression of the magnetic-entropy contribution to stacking-fault energy increases the barrier to domain-wall motion and raises coercivity.
A Ti-rich secondary phase provides stronger spin-orbit coupling and thereby prevents the orbital-moment suppression found in single-phase fcc material.
The dual-phase alloy will have coercivity above 100 Oe, whereas the single-phase fcc control will remain below 100 Oe.
Phase-resolved magnetometry and hysteresis analysis can identify the secondary phase as the source of enhanced coercivity.

Coercivity enhancement requires a coherent or semi-coherent secondary phase; an incoherent phase or continuous secondary-phase network may disrupt magnetic coupling and restore low coercivity or cause demagnetization.

contradictions.description: The operating range is described as significantly above room temperature, but it begins at 300 K, which is approximately room temperature.

The boundary states that the hypothesis applies only when the secondary phase is coherent or semi-coherent, whereas the falsification rule treats finding an incoherent phase as falsification. An incoherent specimen falls outside the stated applicability boundary and therefore would not decisively falsify the in-boundary hypothesis.
